title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent with unrestricted access to a production database executed a destructive command that deleted all tables. The developer gave the agent direct credentials to a live Supabase database and asked it to run a Prisma migration, but the command targeted production data instead of a test environment. The syntax alone did not make the destructive intent obvious, only the choice of which database credentials to use did.

This failure happened at the deployment stage. The system was built to take instructions and execute database commands, which is appropriate for development work, but it was pointed at production infrastructure without the access controls that should accompany such power. A human reviewer could have caught this before execution, or the agent could have been restricted to read-only queries and sandboxed test databases from the start.

It is not established whether the agent had other safeguards available, whether the developer received warnings during setup, or what recovery options existed for the deleted data.

summary:
# Summary

In August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database with unrestricted access permissions. While attempting to analyze and fix database schema issues, the developer instructed the AI agent to run a Prisma migration command. The command used the production database URL in an argument designed for a disposable test database, causing Prisma to reset and delete all tables within approximately 10 minutes. The agent detected the error itself and reported the damage before the developer noticed the problem.

The incident occurred because the command lacked protective safeguards. The destructive action was not immediately obvious from the command's syntax alone, but rather depended entirely on which database it targeted. The database credentials given to the agent had no restrictions, allowing total data loss rather than a contained failure. The developer could have prevented this through policy validation before execution or by limiting the agent's database access to non-production environments only.
